The method

Built 100% by voice. Pasha talked, Claude built.

  1. Say what you want, in plain words. Pasha dictated every request the way he would explain it to a colleague, pauses and half-sentences included. No code or commands were entered by keyboard.
  2. Watch it appear. The page stayed open in his browser and refreshed by itself each time Claude changed it, usually within a minute or two.
  3. React to what you see. Waiting for food should be red. Add a pizza oven. The cooks are hard to click because they keep moving. Each remark became the next change.
  4. Let the AI fill the gaps, and say so. Pasha did not know how many cooks there were or how long anything takes. Claude chose, and listed every choice so it could be corrected.

Seventeen exchanges, about an hour. The slides that follow show what was on the screen at each step.

0:01 · Turn 2

It started with how we would work

… record this conversation in a Markdown file, clearly separating what I said from what you answered … Next, start a local Python web server and build a Hello World HTML page … push your changes to that page so it refreshes and I can see what you're doing.Pasha, lightly trimmed
  • A record. Every exchange goes into a transcript, with Pasha's words kept as spoken.
  • A live page. Pasha keeps one browser tab open, and every change Claude makes shows up there by itself.
  • One minute later both were running, and the first page was on screen.
0:03 – 0:05 · Turns 3 – 4

Four minutes in, we had an interactive page

As a warm-up, Pasha asked for something he could click while watching the page update itself:

  • A pie chart and a table, side by side, with sample weekly sales.
  • Each selects the other: click a sector and its row lights up; click a row and its sector pops out.

One business constraint, stated once. Pasha's corporate laptop does not allow JavaScript libraries from the internet. Claude was using none, and kept it that way for the rest of the project: everything here is hand-built and runs with the network unplugged.

0:07 · Turn 5

Then Pasha described the restaurant from memory

… there are a dozen tables: some round ones for four people, a couple for two, and the rest for six. There's a kitchen somewhere, and I see a couple of waiters. A waiter takes an order and puts up a piece of paper, which I guess a cook picks up; I don't know whether there is one cook or several. Plates come out of the kitchen onto a small table, and a waiter brings them over. On the page, set up an SVG live view and draw the restaurant. Then let's try an animation: waiters moving, people coming in, the kitchen cooking.Pasha, lightly trimmed

That was the whole specification: one spoken paragraph, as a visitor remembers the place. What Pasha did not know, Claude chose and listed, so it could be corrected:

  • The table mix: four round tables for four, two for two, six for six.
  • The kitchen: two cooks, each with a stove, and where the door, the order rail and the pass table sit.
  • Every timing: how often guests arrive, how long they read, cook and eat.
0:14 · Turn 5

Seven minutes later, we had a working restaurant

The first version already ran the whole cycle, from arrival to departure:

  • Dining room: twelve numbered tables and a front door. Guests arrive in parties, walk the aisles to a table that fits, and leave after they eat.
  • Two waiters take the order, carry a paper ticket to the order rail, and later bring plates from the pass table.
  • Two cooks take a ticket off the rail, cook at a stove, and put the plates on the pass.
  • Counters under the picture, and Pause, 1×, 2× and 4×.

One spoken paragraph in, a running model of the business out. It is a simulation, not a drawing: nobody scripted where each guest goes.

0:15 – 0:17 · Turns 6 – 7

We made every table's state readable at a glance

0:17 – 0:18 · Turn 8

We added a coffee machine and a pizza oven

I want to add a coffee machine and a pizza maker to the kitchen.Pasha
  • Pizza oven: a brick oven in the corner. Its mouth glows and a bar fills while a pizza bakes.
  • Coffee machine: by the pass table, with a cup that fills while it brews.
  • The cooks use them. Some orders are pizza and some include coffee, and only one cook can use the oven at a time.

One sentence from Pasha. About a minute later the equipment was on the floor and part of how the kitchen works.

0:19 – 0:23 · Turn 9

We made everything that works selectable

Click any working object and a panel slides out on the right with one "about" card:

  • What it is, its purpose, and why it is here.
  • Right now: a line that updates live, such as "Idle" for the oven or "Taking the order at table 4" for a waiter.
  • One at a time: clicking another object replaces the card; clicking empty floor clears it.

Tables, waiters, cooks, parties, the door, the rail, the pass and the kitchen equipment could all be selected.

0:26 – 0:33 · Turns 10 – 12

We made every order something you can follow

0:26 – 0:38 · Turns 10 – 14

We built a way to pick things that move

0:40 – 0:56 · Turn 15

We finished with a full test suite, also by asking

Pasha asked for tests with full coverage and a single command to run them. Claude wrote them, set up the tools and ran them.

SuiteTestsCoverage
The web server20100%
The page, driven in a real browser48100% (751 lines of JavaScript)
Total68, all passing
  • One command, make test, runs everything in about 13 seconds.
  • Seven screenshots are saved on each run, so a later change to the look of the page shows up.
  • Why it matters: the next change can be checked automatically, not by eye.
0:58 · Finished

What we ended up with: the floor

We did not only draw these objects. We modelled the state each one is in and the activities it takes part in, and the picture follows the model.

  • Tables have a state: free, reading the menu, wants to order, waiting for food, eating. The colour shows it.
  • Parties arrive, queue at the door, walk to a table that fits, order, wait, eat and leave.
  • Waiters take orders, hang tickets on the rail and carry plates from the pass.
  • Cooks take a ticket and work through it: stove dishes, then pizza, then coffee, waiting when the oven is taken.
  • Tickets move from table to rail, cook, pass and back, and keep their own clock.
  • Counters below report the model: guests inside, tickets on the rail, parties served and turned away.
0:58 · Finished

What we ended up with: selection

Everything that does a job in the restaurant can be selected and inspected, one thing at a time.

  • Any instance: a particular table, waiter, cook, party of guests or order ticket, and each stove, the pizza oven, the coffee machine, the front door, the order rail and the pass.
  • Click it on the floor, and it lights up. People and tickets stay selected as they move.
  • Or pick it by name: the magnifying glass lists every object by category, with a filter box.
  • Its card opens in the panel on the right: what it is, its purpose, why it is here, and what it is doing right now.
  • Orders in full: a ticket shows what was ordered, who wrote it and how long it has waited. A table or a party shows its order too.
The result

A whole restaurant, alive, on one page.

It's all done!!! Built in about an hour, 100% by voice: watch guests arrive, order, wait and eat, follow any order through the kitchen, and click anything to learn what it is for.

A model, not a drawingGuests, waiters, cooks and orders each have a state and a job, and the picture follows them.
100% by voiceNo code or commands entered by keyboard. About an hour, start to finish.
Every objectClick a table, a person, a ticket or a stove for what it is, its purpose and what it is doing now.
Every orderTickets carry real items from an invented menu and can be followed from table to rail, cook, pass and back.
Tested68 tests cover every line of the server and of the page's JavaScript.
No installsNo libraries and nothing from the internet. One Python file and one web page.

0:00 – 0:58 · The whole conversation

What it took in tokens

Counted from the session's own log: 14.4 million tokens across 84 requests to the model, all Claude Opus 5.5.

KindTokensWhat it is
Re-read from cache13,961,491The conversation so far, read again on every request. This is 97.3% of the total and is billed at a small fraction of the normal rate.
New input230,381Text entering the conversation for the first time: Pasha's messages, tool results, files and screenshots.
Output164,443Everything Claude wrote: answers, code, commands and its working notes.
Total14,356,315

The total is large because of how a long conversation works, not because much was written. Each of the 84 requests re-reads everything before it, so the same text is counted again and again: on average about 166,000 tokens of history per request.

What that would cost in dollars

About $7.90 on Claude Opus 5.5, the model that ran the session.

ModelRough costNotes
Claude Opus 5.5about $7.90What we used: $2.79 for cache re-reads, $1.84 for new input, $3.29 for output.
Claude Sonnet 5.5about $5.40The same token counts at Sonnet's prices. Its cache-read price is the same as Opus.

Caching is what keeps this small. With no caching, every re-read would be billed as fresh input: about $60 on Opus 5.5.

  • A pricing comparison, not a prediction. Another model would take a different number of steps to do the same work.
  • One assumption: cache writes priced at the one-hour rate, twice the input price.
  • Prices as of October 2026, the same ones used for the NYC Subway Live journey.
Already built

What comes next: Episode 2, The Workflow

Episode 1 shows the restaurant as a room you can watch. Episode 2 takes the same model and turns it into something you can measure and manage.

  • A second view: the work itself, from the door to leaving, with the kitchen's two queues and the staff moving between them.
  • Measurements: an objective, a target and two charts for every object on screen, so you can see where the waiting is.
  • Staffing: add or remove waiters and cooks while it runs, and watch the queues respond.

One step is still ahead of both episodes: the numbers. Every timing in the model is invented. With real figures from the owner, the same model starts answering real questions.
